rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Pertussis is a notifiable infection and public-health guidance covers cases, contacts and outbreaks.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Infants, especially those under 6 months, face the greatest risk of severe complications.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Clinical diagnosis can support notification and action without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Culture, PCR, serology and oral-fluid testing are used in different age and timing circumstances.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Antibiotic treatment is intended to eradicate the organism and reduce onward transmission when given within recommended periods.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Contact management prioritises people at high risk of severe disease and those who may transmit infection to vulnerable infants.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Outbreak guidance includes healthcare and educational settings and provides communication templates.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Vaccination remains a central prevention measure and case management should include review of relevant immunisation status.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: Pertussis risk depends on age, vaccination, contact intensity, setting, symptom timing, testing, treatment and infant exposure.

rows.source: UKHSA pertussis case, contact and outbreak management
rows.verified: UKHSA pertussis evidence is case-, contact-, vaccine-, setting-, laboratory- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: Looped blind cords and chains can present a strangulation hazard to young children.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: New blinds with looped cords must incorporate or be supplied with appropriate child-safety devices.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: Tidies and tensioners should be firmly fixed so cords or chains remain under tension.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: Cleats and spare cord should be positioned and secured outside children's reach.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: Furniture and climbable items should be kept away from blind cords and chains.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: Older blinds may lack newer safety features and should be checked for retrofit controls.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: A failed or detached chain-tidy can allow a cord to become slack and accessible, creating strangulation risk.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: Product-safety reports can require modification, consumer contact, withdrawal or other corrective action for non-compliant blinds.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: Blind-cord risk depends on cord design, loop accessibility, fixing strength, furniture position, child age, supervision and product condition.

rows.source: OPSS blind-cord child-strangulation safety
rows.verified: OPSS blind evidence is product-, installation-, child-, household-, corrective-action- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level strangulation probability.
